topics.title: Imperfect subjunctive
topics.description: Past triggers, polite quisiera, and second-conditional 'si' clauses

guide.intro: The imperfect subjunctive is the past-tense counterpart of the present subjunctive. It shows up whenever a subjunctive trigger sits in a past or conditional clause: 'Quería que vinieras', 'Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría'. Two endings exist — '-ara/-iera' and '-ase/-iese' — and they're 100% interchangeable; the '-ara/-iera' family wins in everyday speech.

sections.text: Formation — the third-person plural shortcut
Take the 'ellos' form of the preterite, drop '-ron', and add the imperfect-subjunctive endings. This works for every verb — regular, irregular, stem-changing, you name it.

sections.text: Trigger: past main clause + subjunctive trigger

Same triggers as the present subjunctive (querer que, dudar que, es necesario que, para que…) but with the main verb in preterite, imperfect, conditional, or pluperfect. The subordinate verb shifts to imperfect subjunctive.

rows.source: Quería que vinieras a la fiesta.
rows.translation: I wanted you to come to the party.
It was necessary that we studied more.
I asked him to help me.
I doubted it was true.

sections.text: Polite 'quisiera'
'Quisiera' (imperfect subjunctive of 'querer') is the politest way to ask for something in Spanish — softer than 'quiero', warmer than 'querría'. Treat it as the fixed polite form: 'I would like…'

rows.translation: I'd like a coffee, please.

rows.source: Quisiéramos reservar una mesa para dos.
rows.translation: We'd like to book a table for two.

sections.text: Si + imperfect subjunctive — hypothetical

The classic 'second conditional': 'If I had X, I would do Y'. Si + imperfect subjunctive in the if-clause, conditional in the result clause. Never use present subjunctive after 'si' — it doesn't exist there.

rows.source: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría por el mundo.
rows.translation: If I had money, I'd travel the world.

rows.source: Si fueras más paciente, te iría mejor.
rows.translation: If you were more patient, things would go better for you.

sections.text: Beware: '-ara/-iera' is the past subjunctive, NOT the conditional. 'Viajara' ≠ 'viajaría'. The if-clause uses subjunctive; the result uses conditional.

topics.title: Conditional perfect
topics.description: Habría + participle for past hypotheticals, regret, and third-conditional 'si' clauses

guide.intro: The conditional perfect — 'habría + participle' — is Spanish's 'would have done' tense. Use it for past hypotheticals you didn't actually do: 'I would have gone, but I was sick'. It's the natural partner of the pluperfect subjunctive in third-conditional 'si' clauses.

sections.text: Formation: habría + past participle
Conditional of 'haber' (habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían) + the past participle of the main verb. Participles don't agree — they always end in -o.

rows.translation: I would have gone
you would have eaten
we would have arrived
they would have told the truth

sections.text: Third conditional — si + pluperfect subj. + conditional perfect
Past unreal: 'If I had X-ed, I would have Y-ed'. The if-clause uses pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle); the result clause uses conditional perfect (habría + participle).

rows.translation: If I had known, I would have come.

rows.source: Si hubieras estudiado más, habrías aprobado.
rows.translation: If you had studied more, you would have passed.

sections.text: Regret and missed opportunity
Conditional perfect is the regret tense. Pair with 'pero' (but) to explain why the action didn't happen.

rows.source: Habría ido a la fiesta, pero estaba enfermo.
rows.translation: I would have gone to the party, but I was sick.

rows.source: Te lo habría dicho, pero no quería preocuparte.
rows.translation: I would have told you, but I didn't want to worry you.

sections.text: Irregular participles
Don't insert anything between 'haber' and the participle. 'Habría ya comido' is wrong — say 'Ya habría comido' or 'Habría comido ya'.

topics.title: Pluperfect (había + participle)
topics.description: Past-before-past in narration and reported speech

guide.intro: The pluperfect — 'había + participle' — is Spanish's 'had done' tense. Use it for the past-before-the-past: actions that happened before another past moment. 'When you called, I had already eaten' → 'Cuando llamaste, yo ya había comido.'

sections.text: Formation
Imperfect of 'haber' (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían) + past participle. Same family of irregular participles as the perfect tenses.

rows.translation: I had already eaten when you arrived.
We had never seen anything like it.
Had you been to Spain before?

sections.text: Sequence in storytelling
When telling a story in the past, the pluperfect drops in to mark something that happened EARLIER than the main timeline. Often paired with 'ya', 'todavía no', 'antes', 'cuando'.

rows.source: Cuando llegó el camarero, ya habíamos pedido.
rows.translation: When the waiter arrived, we had already ordered.

rows.source: No quería ir al cine porque ya había visto la película.
rows.translation: She didn't want to go to the cinema because she had already seen the film.

sections.text: Pluperfect vs preterite vs imperfect
Use preterite for completed past actions, imperfect for background/habits, pluperfect for past-before-past. The three often appear together in narration.

rows.source: Llegué tarde porque había perdido el autobús.
rows.translation: I arrived late because I had missed the bus.

rows.source: Estaba cansado porque no había dormido nada.
rows.translation: He was tired because he hadn't slept at all.

sections.text: English sometimes uses simple past where Spanish prefers pluperfect. 'I told him I saw it' often becomes 'Le dije que lo había visto' in Spanish.

topics.title: Passive voice
topics.description: Ser-passive (formal/news) vs se-passive (natural Spanish) vs impersonal se

guide.intro: Spanish has two passive flavors. The 'ser + participle' passive ('La casa fue construida en 1850') sounds formal — common in journalism. The 'se + verb' passive ('Se construyen muchas casas aquí') is what natives reach for in everyday speech. Master both, and lean on 'se' more often than not.

sections.text: Ser + participle (passive formal)
Like English: subject + ser (conjugated) + participle (agrees in gender/number) + por + agent. Mostly used in writing and news.

rows.source: El libro fue escrito por García Márquez.
rows.translation: The book was written by García Márquez.

rows.source: Las casas son construidas por la empresa local.
rows.translation: The houses are built by the local company.
The agreement will be signed tomorrow.

sections.text: Se + verb (passive 'se')
Most common in spoken Spanish. 'Se' goes before a verb in 3rd person; the verb agrees with the patient (the thing acted on).

rows.translation: Spanish is spoken here.
Used cars are sold (here).

rows.source: Se construyeron muchas casas el año pasado.
rows.translation: Many houses were built last year.

sections.text: Impersonal 'se' (no specific subject)
When you don't want to name a doer at all — 'one', 'people', 'they' — Spanish uses 'se + 3rd singular'. Useful for signs, recipes, instructions.

rows.translation: Smoking is prohibited / No smoking.
How do you say 'hello' in Spanish?
One lives well in Valencia.

sections.text: Quick rule of thumb: if the subject is concrete and you'd just say 'X happened' without caring who did it, use se-passive. Reserve ser-passive for news headlines and formal writing.

items: Se alquila piso — Flat for rent
Se prohíbe pisar el césped — Keep off the grass

topics.title: Expressing opinions
topics.description: Hedge, agree, push back; master indicative/subjunctive triggers

guide.intro: B2 opinion-talk hinges on one rule: doubt and denial trigger subjunctive; certainty doesn't. 'Creo que es verdad' (indicative — I think it's true) vs 'No creo que sea verdad' (subjunctive — I don't think it's true). Master the trigger list, then layer in hedges and counterpoints.

sections.text: Indicative — when you're sure
Affirmative verbs of opinion and certainty take indicative: creo que, pienso que, opino que, estoy seguro de que, es verdad que, es cierto que.

rows.translation: I think you're right.
It's true it rains a lot.
I'm sure he'll come.

sections.text: Subjunctive — when you doubt or deny
Negative versions of those verbs and any expression of doubt, probability, or denial flip to subjunctive: no creo que, dudo que, es probable que, no es cierto que.

rows.translation: I don't think it's true.
I doubt he'll come.
It's likely it'll rain tomorrow.

rows.source: No es cierto que sea tan caro.
rows.translation: It isn't true that it's that expensive.

sections.text: Hedge openers
B2 speakers pad opinions with hedges before committing: 'desde mi punto de vista', 'a mi parecer', 'en mi opinión', 'según yo'. These all take indicative in the dependent clause.

rows.source: Desde mi punto de vista, es un error.
rows.translation: From my point of view, it's a mistake.

rows.source: A mi parecer, no es tan grave.
rows.translation: To my mind, it's not that bad.

sections.text: Agreeing and pushing back

items: No estoy de acuerdo — I don't agree
No tengo claro que… — I'm not sure that… (+ subjunctive!)

sections.text: Question form flips back: '¿Crees que sea verdad?' (subjunctive — doubt embedded) vs '¿Crees que es verdad?' (indicative — neutral question). Many speakers use indicative both ways; subjunctive sounds slightly more doubtful.

guide.intro: Spanish news has its own register: short, dense headlines (often verbless), heavy use of ser-passive, and a stack of attribution phrases ('según fuentes', 'se rumorea', 'al parecer'). Read a few headlines a week and the patterns become second nature.

sections.text: Headline grammar
Spanish headlines often drop the verb of being, leaving a participle + noun: 'Detenidos tres sospechosos', 'Aprobada nueva ley'. Tight, eye-catching, and instantly recognizable as news.

topics.title: Formal Spanish
topics.description: Usted, polite shifts, letters and emails, formal connectors

guide.intro: Formal Spanish lives in business emails, customer-service calls, official letters, and any context where you'd use 'usted' in English-as-Spanish. The hallmarks: 'usted', conditional softeners ('podría', 'sería tan amable'), fixed opening/closing formulas, and a leaner sentence rhythm.

sections.text: Salutations and closings
Letters and emails follow predictable patterns. Open formally, sign off warmly but professionally.

rows.translation: Dear Mr./Mrs. (Surname):
To whom it may concern:
Sincerely,
Kind regards,
Receive my cordial regards,

sections.text: Polite verb shifts
Replace 'puedo', 'quiero', 'necesito' with softer forms — 'podría', 'quisiera', 'le agradecería que…' These signal respect and distance.

rows.source: Quisiera concertar una reunión con usted.
rows.translation: I'd like to arrange a meeting with you.

rows.source: Le agradecería que me confirmara la cita.
rows.translation: I would be grateful if you'd confirm the appointment.

sections.text: Usted vs tú

Use 'usted' (and 'ustedes' in plural) for clients, strangers in formal settings, older people, anyone you don't know well. In Spain, 'tú' has expanded — even between strangers under 40 — but business correspondence stays with 'usted'. Latin America is generally more conservative.

sections.text: When in doubt, default to 'usted'. Switching from 'usted' to 'tú' is easy if the relationship warms up — going the other direction is awkward.

topics.title: Relative clauses
topics.description: Que, el que/el cual, cuyo, donde, lo que; specifying vs explanatory

guide.intro: Relative clauses let you add info about a noun without starting a new sentence. The workhorse is 'que' (works for people and things), but B2 demands more: 'el que / la cual' (after prepositions or for clarity), 'cuyo' (whose), 'donde' (where), and a sharp ear for whether the clause needs commas or not.

sections.text: Specifying (no commas) vs explanatory (with commas)
Specifying ('defining') clauses narrow down which noun you mean — no commas. Explanatory ('non-defining') clauses add bonus info — commas required.

rows.source: El libro que compré ayer es interesante. (specifying — which book?)
rows.translation: The book I bought yesterday is interesting.

rows.source: Mi hermano, que vive en Madrid, viene mañana. (explanatory — extra info)
rows.translation: My brother, who lives in Madrid, is coming tomorrow.

sections.text: Que vs el que / el cual
After a preposition or when 'que' would be ambiguous, switch to 'el que / la que / los que / las que' (or the slightly more formal 'el cual / la cual'). They agree with the noun's gender and number.

rows.source: La amiga con la que viajo es de Bogotá.
rows.translation: The friend I'm traveling with is from Bogotá.

rows.source: El proyecto del que te hablé está aprobado.
rows.translation: The project I told you about has been approved.

rows.source: Habló con el director, el cual decidió ayudar.
rows.translation: He spoke with the director, who decided to help.

sections.text: Cuyo — whose
'Cuyo' agrees with the noun it MODIFIES (not the owner). It's formal — often replaced in speech with 'que su…'.

rows.source: El autor cuyo libro leí ganó el premio.
rows.translation: The author whose book I read won the prize.

rows.source: La señora cuyos hijos son tus amigos vive al lado.
rows.translation: The lady whose kids are your friends lives next door.

sections.text: Donde — where
'Donde' replaces 'en el que / en la que' when referring to a place. Use 'a donde' for direction.

rows.source: La ciudad donde nací es muy pequeña.
rows.translation: The city where I was born is very small.

rows.source: El restaurante a donde vamos cierra a las 11.
rows.translation: The restaurant we're going to closes at 11.

sections.text: Spanish does NOT drop the relative pronoun like English does. 'The book I bought' must be 'el libro QUE compré', not 'el libro compré'.

topics.title: Modal perfects
topics.description: Should have, could have, must have — debería/podría/debe de haber + participle

guide.intro: Modal perfects — 'should have done', 'could have done', 'might have done' — pair a modal verb (deber, poder, tener que) with 'haber + participle'. They're the main way Spanish expresses past obligation, possibility, and missed-opportunity regret.

sections.text: Should have / shouldn't have
Use 'deber' (or 'tener que') in the conditional + 'haber + participle' for past obligation that wasn't met.

rows.translation: I should have studied more.
You shouldn't have said it.
I should have called earlier.

sections.text: Could have
'Poder' (in conditional) + 'haber + participle' = 'could have'. Often used for missed opportunities or possibilities.

rows.translation: We could have gone to the cinema.
You could have told me sooner.

sections.text: Must have / may have (probability about the past)
'Deber de haber + participle' (or just conditional perfect 'habría…') expresses 'must have' / 'probably did'. 'Puede que haya + participle' expresses 'may have'.

rows.translation: He must have already left.
They may have arrived.
It must have been a mistake.

sections.text: Word order tip: with reflexive/object pronouns, you can attach them to 'haber' or place them before 'debería' — 'Debería habérselo dicho' OR 'Se lo debería haber dicho'. Both correct.

topics.title: Debate and disagreement
topics.description: Formal disagreement: discrepo, con todo respeto, aunque + subj., signposting

guide.intro: Formal disagreement in Spanish balances directness with respect. The key vocabulary: 'discrepo' (I disagree, formal), 'con todo respeto' (with all due respect), 'permítame discrepar' (allow me to differ), plus hedges, qualifiers, and signposts.

sections.text: Polite disagreement
Direct contradiction comes across as rude. Layer your dissent — acknowledge the other view, then introduce yours.

rows.source: Con todo respeto, no comparto esa opinión.
rows.translation: With all due respect, I don't share that opinion.
I disagree on this point.
Allow me to qualify that.
I understand your position, but…

sections.text: Signposts for structuring a debate

items: En primer lugar… — In the first place…
Por otra parte… — On the other hand…
Cabe destacar que… — It's worth highlighting that…
Es preciso señalar que… — It must be pointed out that…
A modo de conclusión… — By way of conclusion…

sections.text: Hedge softeners

Even when sharp, Spanish debate softens with hedges like 'en cierta medida' (to some extent), 'hasta cierto punto' (up to a point), 'no del todo' (not entirely). They let you concede without conceding everything.

rows.translation: I agree up to a point.

rows.translation: That's true to some extent.
I'm not entirely convinced.

sections.text: Concession then pushback
The classic move: 'aunque + subjunctive, X is still true'. This lets you grant the opponent's point while resisting it.

rows.translation: Even if you're right about that, I still think…

sections.text: Si-clause cheat sheet

items: Real: Si + present + present/future → 'Si llueve, no salgo'
Hypothetical (2nd cond.): Si + imperf. subj. + conditional → 'Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría'
Past unreal (3rd cond.): Si + plup. subj. + conditional perfect → 'Si hubiera sabido, habría venido'

sections.text: Indicative vs subjunctive after 'que'

items: Certainty / fact → indicative: 'Creo que es verdad', 'Es evidente que llueve'
Doubt / denial / emotion / influence → subjunctive: 'No creo que sea verdad', 'Es importante que estudies'
Past trigger → imperf. subj.: 'Quería que vinieras'

sections.text: When you're stuck, ask: am I expressing FACT or REACTION? Fact → indicative. Reaction (doubt, emotion, judgment, will) → subjunctive.
